title: Capstone: Thesis
description: The capstone of the program. Each student chooses a thesis topic in biblical studies, theology, church history or ministry, and works through the stages of a real research project with the AI tutor as a thesis adviser: choosing and narrowing a topic, building a bibliography from the library, writing a detailed outline, writing a full draft, and revising it into a final paper. Every stage is submitted and graded on the program rubric (thesis, exegesis, use of sources, theological reasoning, clarity), with feedback and unlimited revision.

lessons.title: Choosing and Narrowing a Topic

objectives.text: Choose a thesis topic that is significant, manageable and answerable from Scripture and the library.
Narrow a broad subject into a single research question.
State a working thesis in one clear, arguable sentence.

quiz_bank.question: Proverbs 18:17 warns that the first to present his case seems right until
What is the difference between a topic, a research question and a thesis statement?
quiz_bank.answer_key: A topic is a broad subject area; a research question is the single specific question the paper will answer within that topic; a thesis statement is a one-sentence arguable answer to that question that the paper defends with evidence.

quiz_bank.question: Why is a narrow, manageable thesis better than a broad one?
quiz_bank.answer_key: A narrow thesis can be researched thoroughly and argued in depth with real evidence from Scripture and sources in the space available, while a broad one produces a shallow survey with no clear argument.

lessons.paper_prompt: Submit your thesis proposal (500-800 words). Include: (1) your topic and why it matters; (2) your specific research question; (3) a working thesis statement in one sentence; (4) the main Scripture passages you will examine, with references; (5) at least three library works you expect to use (cite as Author, Title, section); and (6) the scope - what your thesis will and will not cover. The grade evaluates whether the proposal sets up a focused, arguable and well-grounded project.

objectives.text: Perform careful exegesis of the key passages for the thesis, using the original languages where possible.
Find and evaluate relevant sources in the library across traditions and centuries.
Build an annotated bibliography that fairly represents differing views.

quiz_bank.question: Explain the difference between primary and secondary sources and give an example of each.
quiz_bank.answer_key: Primary sources are original texts, such as Scripture or a church father's own writing (for example, Athanasius' On the Incarnation); secondary sources interpret primary sources, such as a commentary or a church history (for example, Schaff's History of the Christian Church).

quiz_bank.question: Why must a thesis present opposing views fairly?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Honesty and charity require representing others accurately, and a thesis is only persuasive if it answers the strongest form of the opposing arguments rather than a caricature; fair engagement also shows where Christians genuinely disagree.

lessons.paper_prompt: Submit an exegesis and annotated bibliography (1,000-1,500 words). Part one: a focused exegesis of the single most important Scripture passage for your thesis - its context, structure, key words (with original-language notes where you can), and meaning. Part two: an annotated bibliography of at least five library sources (cite as Author, Title, section), each with two or three sentences summarizing its argument and explaining how it bears on your thesis. Include at least one source that disagrees with your working thesis.

lessons.title: Outlining the Argument

objectives.text: Organize research into a logical argument that supports the thesis.
Write a detailed outline with a claim, evidence and source for each section.
Anticipate the strongest objections and plan responses.

quiz_bank.question: Why should a thesis outline include objections and replies?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Engaging objections shows the writer understands the debate, tests the thesis, answers the strongest counterarguments fairly, and makes the argument more honest and persuasive, following models like Aquinas' objection-and-reply method.

quiz_bank.question: What makes an argument's structure logical?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Each section advances a clear claim that supports the thesis, in an order where earlier points lay the foundation for later ones, with evidence for each claim and transitions showing how they connect, leading to a conclusion that follows from the evidence.

lessons.paper_prompt: Submit a detailed thesis outline (800-1,200 words). Begin with your final research question and thesis statement. Then give each major section with: its main claim, the Scripture passages and library sources (Author, Title, section) that support it, and how it advances the argument. Include a section that states at least two serious objections to your thesis and outlines your reply. End with a short statement of your conclusion and its significance for the church.

lessons.title: Writing the Draft

objectives.text: Write a full draft that develops the thesis with exegesis, sources and theological reasoning.
Integrate and cite sources accurately, quoting and paraphrasing honestly.
Write with clarity, charity and appropriate academic style.

quiz_bank.question: What should the introduction and conclusion of a thesis accomplish?
quiz_bank.answer_key: The introduction presents the research question, explains why it matters, and states the thesis and the plan of the paper; the conclusion summarizes how the evidence supports the thesis, addresses its limits, and draws out its implications for theology and the church.

quiz_bank.question: How should sources be integrated into a thesis?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Sources should be introduced, quoted or paraphrased accurately and cited, then explained and evaluated in the writer's own words so they serve the argument, rather than being strung together or used to replace the writer's own reasoning.

lessons.paper_prompt: Submit the full draft of your thesis (3,000-5,000 words). It should include an introduction with your thesis statement, body sections that develop your argument through careful exegesis of Scripture and engagement with at least five library sources (cite as Author, Title, section), a fair treatment of at least two objections, and a conclusion that states the significance of your findings. This draft is graded on the full rubric; use the feedback to plan your revision.

lessons.title: Revision and Final Thesis

objectives.text: Revise the draft in response to feedback, strengthening argument, evidence and clarity.
Check every Scripture reference and citation for accuracy.
Submit a polished final thesis and reflect on what the project taught you.

quiz_bank.question: What should a writer do when receiving critical feedback on a draft?
quiz_bank.answer_key: Receive it humbly as help, identify the main weaknesses in argument, evidence and clarity, rethink and restructure where needed rather than only making surface changes, verify references and citations, and resubmit a stronger paper.

quiz_bank.question: What does Augustine's Retractations teach about the scholar's character?
quiz_bank.answer_key: It shows intellectual humility and honesty - a willingness to reexamine one's own work, admit mistakes and correct them publicly for the sake of truth and the good of readers.

lessons.paper_prompt: Submit your final thesis (4,000-6,000 words), revised in light of the feedback on your draft. It must present a clear thesis, careful exegesis of the key passages, engagement with at least six library sources (cite as Author, Title, section) including at least one opposing view treated fairly, sound theological reasoning, and a clear, well-organized argument. Check every Scripture reference and citation. End with a one-paragraph reflection on how the project has shaped your understanding and your ministry. Completing this paper completes the program.
